records.exact_task: A copper strip, graphite sheet and crystalline salt all transmit current in at least one tested state. Copper conducts when solid, graphite much better along the sheet than across stacked layers, and salt only after melting. Explain the different carrier mechanisms and why an identical current reading is not evidence of identical bonding.
records.protected_W: Connect three distinct microscopic carrier mechanisms to state/direction evidence and reject the equal-current inference.
records.worked_answer: Copper: mobile electrons through metallic structure. Graphite: delocalised electrons within covalent layers, anisotropic transport. Salt: ions fixed in ordinary lattice, mobile after melting. Equal readings can arise from distinct carrier types and depend on sample geometry and contacts. The shared observable is charge transport, not bond identity.
records.boundary_prompt: Could a dry salt conduct weakly through defects? Explain why this would not automatically establish metallic bonding.
records.boundary_answer: Yes, defects can permit ionic motion in some solids. Carrier identity requires independent evidence, not a binary conductivity test.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Connect carriers, structures and common response

hint_evidence.H1: Sort the observations by material, physical state and direction.
hint_evidence.H2: Ask what charged species could move in each structure, not whether the material looks shiny.
hint_evidence.H3: Construct a carrier–structure–observation chain for each material; compare what an equal instrument reading does and does not constrain.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: In a hypothetical survey, dry X and dry Y are electrical insulators. X dissolves to yield equal amounts of positive and negative monovalent ions and conducts; Y reacts with water to yield equal amounts of ions and also conducts. A report identifies both original solids as ionic because the solutions have the same ion concentration. Combine the particle and experimental evidence to evaluate this conclusion and propose a way to distinguish the initial materials.
records.protected_W: Integrate before/after species inventories and independent solid evidence, explaining the underdetermination.
records.worked_answer: Both final liquids have mobile ions; X may be an ionic solid whose pre-existing ions separate, while Y may be molecular and form ions by reaction with water. The equal concentrations do not determine original structures or identical conductivity (mobility matters). Distinguish initial solid by structural/composition evidence or a suitable nonreactive-solvent/melt test where feasible. Do not infer initial bonding solely from final ions.
records.boundary_prompt: If Y forms ions only in water, would lack of conductivity in a nonreactive solvent uniquely prove covalent bonding?
records.boundary_answer: No. Insolubility and limited dissociation could also make an ionic compound nonconducting in that solvent.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Integrate alternative histories and independent test

hint_evidence.H1: Make separate before-water and after-water evidence columns.
hint_evidence.H2: Distinguish ions already in the solid from ions created by reaction; consider mobility separately.
hint_evidence.H3: Sketch two possible particle histories ending in the same ion inventory. Identify which missing measurement would separate them.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: A clean iron strip is immersed in a Cu²⁺ solution. In a simplified record 0.040 mol Fe²⁺ forms, 0.030 mol Cu is recovered and no other products are measured. Explain how the two half-reactions couple, whether the recorded copper amount accounts for all electron transfer, and why the blue colour fading alone is insufficient.
records.protected_W: Explain coupled electron transfer and independently reconcile the observed species amounts.
records.worked_answer: Fe→Fe²⁺+2e⁻ supplies 0.080 mol electrons; Cu²⁺+2e⁻→Cu consumes 0.060 mol. 0.020 mol electrons unaccounted if measurements exact. Incomplete Cu recovery, another electron acceptor or measurement error are alternatives; colour changes alone do not identify or quantify products. Sulfate is spectator if present.
records.boundary_prompt: If Fe instead forms Fe³⁺ and Cu is the sole acceptor, how much Cu is formed per 0.020 mol Fe?

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Explain transfer, ledger discrepancy and observation limit

hint_evidence.H1: Write the initial and final species for each metal.
hint_evidence.H2: Use oxidation-state changes to determine electrons transferred per metal atom.
hint_evidence.H3: Set up an electron ledger using the recorded amounts; compare totals and distinguish recovered material from formed material.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: Clean A displaces B²⁺; clean B displaces C²⁺; clean D displaces B²⁺. A coated D strip gives no deposit in A²⁺. Draw the supported partial order, list unresolved pairs, and choose the smallest additional controlled comparison needed to decide the most reactive metal.
records.protected_W: Select a partial-order graph and identify the missing edge controlling the maximal element.
records.worked_answer: Edges A>B, B>C, D>B; transitivity gives A>C and D>C under comparable conditions. A vs D unresolved; coated negative does not resolve it. These are the two possible maximal metals. A controlled clean A/D comparison with suitable verification can decide which is above; reciprocal test if negative is ambiguous. No ranking of rates.
records.boundary_prompt: If clean A displaces D²⁺, what total order follows under assumptions?

concept_model_selection.evidence: Choose partial-order rather than total ranking

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Infer transitive edges and minimal discrimination

hint_evidence.H1: Separate positive tests from the coated result.
hint_evidence.H2: Draw directed edges from each displacing metal to the displaced metal.
hint_evidence.H3: Trace paths through the graph and find nodes with no incoming edge; leave their ordering undecided until you select a controlled test.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: An ideal salt L contains L²⁺ and X⁻. A dry crystal gives negligible current; molten sample conducts; aqueous solution of the same nominal mass gives lower current than a more dilute solution of a different salt. Explain all three observations without claiming that nominal mass or ion count alone controls conductivity.
records.protected_W: Explain phase-dependent transport and distinguish nominal amount from carrier mobility and concentration.
records.worked_answer: LX₂ formula neutral; ions in ordinary crystal confined, mobile in melt. Dissolved ions are mobile but different salts may differ in actual concentration, degree of dissociation, carrier charge/mobility, temperature and geometry. Nominal mass not number of ions. Compare matched geometry/temperature, concentration and species before ranking.
records.boundary_prompt: If both solutions have equal ion concentration, must conductivity be equal?
records.boundary_answer: No; mobilities, charge magnitudes and interactions differ.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Explain three observations and reject comparison

hint_evidence.H1: Identify which phases contain potentially mobile ions.
hint_evidence.H2: Check what mass can tell you without molar mass or dissolved fraction.
hint_evidence.H3: Connect each phase to carrier mobility and list controlled variables for the two solution readings.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: Two ideal salts A₂X₃ and BY₂ dissociate completely; A is 3+, X is 2−, B is 2+, Y is 1−. Equal volumes contain 0.010 mol of each salt. Construct a charge-and-particle ledger before mixing, then after mixing if only B²⁺ and X²⁻ precipitate quantitatively as BX. Find the remaining dissolved amounts and explain why current cannot be calculated from charge balance alone.
records.protected_W: Integrate formula-unit dissociation, precipitation and independent charge check.
records.worked_answer: Initial A³⁺ .020, X²⁻ .030, B²⁺ .010, Y⁻ .020 mol. BX precipitates .010 mol, leaving X²⁻ .020, A³⁺ .020, Y⁻ .020, B²⁺ 0. Charge equivalents +.060 and −(.040+.020)=−.060. Conductivity depends on mobility, concentration/volume and interactions, not neutrality alone.
records.boundary_prompt: If 0.040 mol BY₂ is mixed instead, how much B²⁺ remains after complete BX precipitation?
records.boundary_answer: 0.010 mol B²⁺ remains; .030 mol X²⁻ limits.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Combine reaction, limiting species and charge check

hint_evidence.H1: Expand each salt formula into a before-mixing ion inventory.
hint_evidence.H2: Identify which two ions form the neutral precipitate and determine their consumption ratio.
hint_evidence.H3: Make initial/change/final rows for every ion; check positive and negative charge equivalents after the reaction.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: A proposal treats two hypothetical oxide feeds M₂O and NO identically with carbon because both equations can be balanced. M is sodium-like and N zinc-like. Explain why balanced stoichiometry is necessary but insufficient, compare plausible extraction mechanisms and identify what additional evidence is required before predicting actual recovery.
records.protected_W: Explain difference between formal balance, energetic feasibility and recovery for two ore models.
records.worked_answer: Atom balance describes amounts, not thermodynamic feasibility or rates. Highly reactive M typically needs electrolysis of a suitable molten salt; less reactive N oxide may be reduced by carbon/CO in appropriate conditions. Electrolysis supplies external electrical energy; chemical reduction transfers electrons from reductant. Need oxide stability/conditions, separation, side reaction and recovery evidence. No practical procedure implied.
records.boundary_prompt: A molten-salt electrolysis equation is balanced; does that prove all deposited metal is recovered?
records.boundary_answer: No. Side reactions and recovery losses may occur.

hint_evidence.H1: Separate the written equation from the observation that a metal is actually obtained.
hint_evidence.H2: Compare where electrons come from in a chemical reductant versus electrolysis.
hint_evidence.H3: Build two causal chains from ore stability to reduction and collection; specify what information each chain lacks.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: Two ore feeds contain only ZnS, ZnCO₃ and inert quartz. Feed P yields 0.18 mol ZnO after complete conversion; its conversion gases contain 0.06 mol SO₂. Feed Q yields the same total gas amount but contains twice as much carbonate as P. Can Q have the same total ZnO under these assumptions? Infer P composition, construct Q's implied composition or demonstrate impossibility, then select the measurement that distinguishes the feeds.
records.protected_W: Select a feasible inverse ore-composition model, test nonnegative amounts and reject inconsistent data.
records.worked_answer: For P: ZnS=.06 mol; ZnCO₃=.18−.06=.12 mol. Each precursor yields one conversion gas per ZnO: total .18 mol. Q carbonate=.24 mol, exceeding total .18 mol available; Q would require negative sulfide (−.06 mol), impossible. Hence the records cannot all hold. Independently measure CO₂ or total ZnO and verify completeness; quartz is inert by assumption. Equations 2ZnS+3O₂→2ZnO+2SO₂; ZnCO₃→ZnO+CO₂.
records.boundary_prompt: Can a Q feed with .09 mol carbonate and total .18 mol conversion gas fit?
records.boundary_answer: Yes: .09 mol ZnS and .09 mol ZnCO₃, .18 mol ZnO; distinct gas compositions.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select inverse feasibility model rather than forward recipe

representation_translation.evidence: Convert gas species and total into two ledgers

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Infer P then test Q's consistency and choose discriminator

hint_evidence.H1: Separate feed P's measured species from Q's comparison.
hint_evidence.H2: Use one balanced conversion equation per precursor and identify a conserved total.
hint_evidence.H3: Sketch an unknown-amount ledger for each feed; test whether the implied entries could be physically possible before drawing a conclusion.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: Author scaffold leaves decisive result; blind review HOLD.

records.exact_task: Two pure white oxides X and Y both react with acid; only X forms a soluble anionic hydroxo species in strong aqueous base. Explain the difference using ZnO as a model for X and MgO for Y. Write the appropriate acid and base equations, and explain why using excess base rather than weak alkali matters.
records.protected_W: Explain two acid/base mechanisms through phase-appropriate species and evidence.
records.worked_answer: ZnO+2H⁺→Zn²⁺+H₂O; ZnO+2OH⁻+H₂O→[Zn(OH)₄]²⁻. MgO+2H⁺→Mg²⁺+H₂O; no analogous simple strong-base dissolution expected under stated ordinary model. Amphoterism requires both reagent contexts, sufficient conditions and product evidence; a negative weak-base observation is insufficient.
records.boundary_prompt: Would acid dissolution of CaO alone identify an amphoteric oxide?
records.boundary_answer: No; it supports basic behaviour but not reaction with base.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Link both reaction contexts to classification

hint_evidence.H1: Identify which observation the two oxides share and which differs.
hint_evidence.H2: For acid, track H⁺ and oxide oxygen; for base, use the stated hydroxo species model.
hint_evidence.H3: Balance atoms and charge in each candidate equation, then use the observed product to explain the classification.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: A hypothetical mixture contains only MgO and ZnO. Excess acid consumes 0.100 mol H⁺; under an ideal selective strong-base model ZnO alone consumes 0.040 mol OH⁻ forming [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻. Determine the amounts of each oxide, predict total mass using MgO=40 and ZnO=81 g/mol, and explain what would invalidate this inference.
records.protected_W: Integrate two selective reaction ledgers with independent mass check.
records.worked_answer: Both oxides consume 2 H⁺ per mole so total .050 mol. ZnO consumes 2 OH⁻ per mole => .020 mol ZnO and .030 mol MgO. Mass .020×81+.030×40=2.82 g. Assumes complete separate reactions, selective base dissolution, no other acid/base-consuming species; measured mass is an independent check.
records.boundary_prompt: If actual mass is 3.00 g, is the model proven correct by titrant amounts alone?
records.boundary_answer: No. Investigate impurity, incomplete reaction or measurement error; independent mass disagrees.

hint_evidence.H1: Write separate acid-equivalent relationships for both oxides.
hint_evidence.H2: Use the stated selective base reaction to obtain an independent relationship.
hint_evidence.H3: Set up two equations in the unknown oxide amounts, then compare the calculated total mass with an independent measurement.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: In matched iron coupons, A is wet and oxygenated, B is wet and deoxygenated, C is dry with oxygen, and D is wet and oxygenated but has poor ionic conductivity. Explain why electron transfer requires two coupled processes and predict which comparison isolates oxygen, moisture and ionic transport; distinguish observation from guaranteed rate.
records.protected_W: Connect local half-reactions to three controlled comparisons and limit rate prediction.
records.worked_answer: A vs B tests oxygen; A vs C tests moisture if other conditions matched; A vs D tests ionic transport. Fe oxidation releases electrons, oxygen reduction consumes them in ordinary neutral aerated rusting; water enables ionic transport. D may corrode more slowly but exact rate needs measurements. Other acceptors can enable corrosion without oxygen.
records.boundary_prompt: Can oxygen-free acidic water corrode iron through a different cathodic reaction?
records.boundary_answer: Yes; H⁺ reduction can be a cathodic process under suitable conditions, so no oxygen does not mean all corrosion impossible.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Explain reaction coupling and controlled inference

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Other cathodic reactions and rate uncertainty

hint_evidence.H1: Make a variable table for the four coupons.
hint_evidence.H2: Identify a source of electrons and a possible electron-consuming process.
hint_evidence.H3: Connect the electron path and ionic path, then choose paired comparisons changing one variable at a time.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: H3 supplies a scaffold, not the completed conclusion/ledger. Independent review pending.

records.exact_task: Two scratched iron specimens carry different conductive coatings. Coating X is electrically connected to iron and loses mass while exposed iron corrodes little; Y is connected and remains almost unchanged while corrosion concentrates at the iron scratch. A third specimen has X physically nearby but insulated from iron. Choose barrier or galvanic models for each, predict the insulated specimen, and identify a control that distinguishes sacrificial protection from a noble coating.
records.protected_W: Infer which electrode is sacrificial from contrasting mass-loss patterns, then test electronic continuity.
records.worked_answer: X fits preferential oxidation supplying electrons to iron; Y may be a more noble coating with exposed iron anodic, not protective at a scratch. A nearby insulated X cannot provide electronic galvanic protection, though other environmental effects are possible. Compare equal exposed area, electrolyte and contact; measure coating mass loss and electrode potential/current direction. No rate guarantee from observations alone.
records.boundary_prompt: If a noble coating is completely intact, can it still protect as a barrier?
records.boundary_answer: Yes, intact coverage may exclude reactants; scratch exposes a different galvanic situation.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select barrier versus two galvanic models

representation_translation.evidence: Translate mass loss to electrode roles

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Infer mechanism, predict insulation, choose control

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Conductive noble coating may accelerate exposed iron

hint_evidence.H1: Distinguish where material loss occurs in the two connected samples.
hint_evidence.H2: Consider the direction of electron flow if either coating or iron oxidises.
hint_evidence.H3: Draw separate metal/contact/electrolyte paths for X and Y; use the insulated case to test your chosen mechanism.
hint_evidence.author_non_disclosure_check: Author scaffold leaves decisive result; blind review HOLD.
